Let n be a positive integer. We prove the result with c=2/7 and d=2.

For n≥3, call each set of three consecutive cells in one row or column a potential triple. There are

T=2n(n-2)

potential triples. In any terminal configuration, every potential triple contains a removed stamp; otherwise those three stamps could be removed as another block.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting columns must lie within two positions of the block's starting column. Each of its three cells belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, so the block meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples altogether. The same bound holds for a vertical block.

Consequently, if k blocks produce a terminal configuration, then

14k≥2n(n-2),

so

k≥n(n-2)/7=n²/7-2n/7.

This applies in particular to k=b(n). For n=1,2, we have b(n)=0, and the same inequality remains valid. Hence the lower bound holds with c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first suppose n≥5. Let m=5⌊n/5⌋ and r=n-m, so 0≤r≤4. In every row, partition the first m columns into consecutive groups of five. In each such group remove one horizontal block as follows:

• in every odd-numbered row, remove the first three cells of the group;
• in every even-numbered row, remove the last three cells of the group.

These blocks are pairwise disjoint, and their number is

n(m/5)≤n²/5.

No horizontal triple lying wholly in the first m columns remains, because in each row every run of unremoved cells there has length at most two. Moreover, no vertical triple in any of the first m columns remains: in positions 1 and 2 of each five-column group every odd row is removed, in position 3 every row is removed, and in positions 4 and 5 every even row is removed. Every three consecutive rows include both parities.

Therefore every triple still available after these removals lies entirely in the strip S consisting of columns m-1,m,…,n. Indeed, a horizontal triple not contained in the first m columns starts no earlier than column m-1, while an available vertical triple must have column greater than m. The strip has width r+2≤6.

Now repeatedly remove any available block until none remains. Removing stamps cannot create a new available triple, so every additional block lies in S. Since these additional blocks are disjoint and each uses three cells of S, their number is at most

|S|/3=(r+2)n/3≤2n.

Thus

b(n)≤n²/5+2n.

For 1≤n<5, a greedy maximal collection contains at most n²/3 blocks, and

n²/3≤n²/5+2n.

Hence the upper bound also holds for these n. Therefore, for every positive integer n,

n²/7-(2/7)n≤b(n)≤n²/5+2n,

which proves the theorem.

problem.theorem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).

Every required string, including reason, must contain non-whitespace explanatory text even when the answer is a proof or no defects are found. Use empty arrays for absent list items.
